title: Forgive readily (2:10)
hookLine: the one asked should not be cruel, but forgive with a whole heart
tomorrow: what if the person you hurt is gone?

cards: The apology finally comes, and it's a good one. Specific, no excuses, clearly rewritten more than once. And there's a small, sweet power in holding it a while.
Letting them wait. So when you're the one asked, how fast should you say yes? Maimonides answers in the very next halakhah, and he doesn't leave much room for the waiting game.

teach.b: It is forbidden, he writes, to be cruel and refuse to be won over. A person should be easy to appease and hard to anger.

teach.h: A WHOLE HEART, A WILLING SOUL.
teach.b: When the one who wronged you asks, forgive with a whole heart and a willing soul, even if they hurt you badly, without revenge and without a grudge. He roots it in the Torah: "Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge."
One honest note: he's speaking to someone asked sincerely, by a person who has done the work.
Forgiving readily doesn't mean pretending a serious harm was small. Now look at the whole week as one road. Leave, regret, resolve.
Let go first. I am someone else now. Admit it to them.
Repair first. Ask again. Six steps for the one who did wrong.
And then a seventh, for the one who was wronged: forgive readily.
Return takes two people, and Maimonides gives each of them a job.

how: Before Yom Kippur some Jews say aloud that they forgive anyone who wronged them, and the bedtime Shema in some prayer books includes a line forgiving others; both follow the ideal of being easy to appease.

o: forgive anyone, whether or not they ever ask you
forgive yourself before you forgive anyone else
forgive quickly and fully when someone sincerely asks

games.q: the one who's asked — tap the pairs.
p: to be cruel and refuse to be won over
thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge

s: it's fair to make someone who sincerely apologized wait it out
Maimonides calls refusing to be won over cruel: forgive with a whole heart and a willing soul.
Maimonides roots forgiving in the Torah's ban on revenge and grudges
Leviticus: thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge.
forgiving readily means saying the harm wasn't a big deal
it means no revenge and no grudge once someone sincerely asks, not pretending the harm was small.

games.q: a teammate who cost your team the final apologizes to you, sincerely, in front of the bench. part of you wants to say 'we'll see.' what does 2:10 point to?
o: accept it now, fully, with no 'we'll see' kept in your pocket.
say 'we'll see,' so they know you'll be watching from now on.
say 'it's fine' out loud, and keep score quietly for later.
games.why: Maimonides: be easy to appease, and forgive with a whole heart, without revenge or a grudge. 'it's fine' with a ledger isn't a whole heart.

practice: Listen for the longest sound you can hear: a fan, traffic, the hum of a fridge. Bring to mind one small grudge you're keeping against someone who already asked.
Each time the sound fades or changes, let your grip on it loosen a little more.

wordCard.voice: Forgive readily: easy to appease, hard to anger. When someone sincerely asks, forgive with a whole heart, without revenge or a grudge.

orig.note: Hebrew: with a whole heart, how Maimonides says to forgive.

carryVoice: Keep this one: forgive readily, because being asked is its own kind of turn. A week of return, complete.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:10 (not to be cruel; easy to appease, hard to anger; forgive with a whole heart, without revenge or grudge)

sources.q: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge
